track.name: fpa-reporting
track.label: FP&A & Management Reporting
track.summary: Build the skills of a finance business partner — from budgeting and variance analysis to polished management accounts and financial storytelling that influences leadership decisions.

phases.title: FP&A Fundamentals
phases.description: Understand what FP&A actually does inside a company — the planning cycle, the relationship with the business, and how FP&A differs from accounting.

phases.title: Budgeting & Forecasting
phases.description: Build zero-based and driver-based budgets, replace static annual plans with rolling forecasts, and model the assumptions that connect business activity to financial outcomes.

phases.title: Variance Analysis
phases.description: Explain the gap between plan and actual — produce waterfall charts, bridge analyses, and root-cause narratives that answer 'why did we miss?' in plain language.

phases.title: Management Accounts
phases.description: Structure a monthly P&L pack from contribution margin to EBITDA, build KPI dashboards, and produce the management accounts that finance teams deliver to leadership.

phases.title: Financial Storytelling
phases.description: Turn numbers into narratives — choose the right chart, build a compelling exec-ready slide, and frame financial results in the context of the decisions leadership needs to make.

phases.title: FP&A Tools & Automation
phases.description: Use Excel and Google Sheets to their full potential, automate data prep with Power Query, and get oriented with enterprise FP&A platforms like Anaplan.

phases.title: Start Here: Excel Essentials
phases.description: FP&A lives in spreadsheets. These basics — formulas, core functions, lookups and tables — come first, and are credited automatically if you have already done them elsewhere.

topics.title: What FP&A Does
topics.description: Map the FP&A function — budgeting, forecasting, reporting, and business partnering — and understand how it sits between accounting and strategy.

steps.d: Draw a diagram showing FP&A's role — budget planning, monthly reporting, forecasting, and business partnering — and where each function sits in the planning cycle.
Explain why the controller records historical transactions (accounting) while FP&A forecasts future outcomes (FP&A), and why a company needs both.

steps.t: Identify FP&A ownership of each process
steps.d: For each step in an annual planning cycle (targets, budget, close, forecast, review), note who owns it — FP&A, business unit, or finance shared.
Ask someone in an FP&A role about their monthly close, their largest headache, and what % of their time is spent on reporting vs. business partnering.
Write a one-page memo explaining what the FP&A team provides and why it matters — speed to decision, accuracy of forecast, insight into unit economics.

topics.title: Finance Business Partnering
topics.description: Learn what it means to be a business partner rather than a reporter — translating financial data into actionable insight for operational leaders.

steps.t: Identify a business question that needs financial insight
steps.d: Find a question from an operational leader ('Should we open a new office?') and define the financial metrics that should drive the decision.

steps.t: Translate a business metric to financial impact
steps.d: Take an operational metric like 'customer churn up 5%' and calculate what that means for recurring revenue, CAC payback, and cash flow.

steps.t: Build a simple model of a business driver
steps.d: Create a spreadsheet that shows how changing units sold or price per unit affects gross margin and EBITDA.

steps.t: Present a business case for a decision
steps.d: Prepare a one-slide financial summary that shows a business unit the breakeven point, payback period, and annual profit impact of a proposed investment.
Present your analysis to a business leader and ask whether the financial framing matches their intuition, or if you've missed a key driver.

topics.title: The Planning Cycle
topics.description: Follow the annual planning cycle from target-setting and budgeting through monthly close, forecasting, and strategic review — and see where FP&A owns each step.

steps.d: Document the sequence of events at your company or a sample company — goal-setting in Q3, budget due in October, monthly close in first week, forecast in second week.
For each phase (targets, budgeting, close, forecasting, review), write down which team owns the process — FP&A, business units, or finance.

steps.t: List key decisions at each gate
steps.d: Note what decisions happen at each step (approve targets, adjust budget, approve forecast, adjust spending) and when leadership meets to make them.
Identify where the cycle creates stress (too little time to close, conflicting targets across regions) and propose process changes.
Create a Gantt chart or calendar showing the planning cycle month by month, with who submits what by when, and present it to your team.

topics.title: Zero-Based Budgeting
topics.description: Build every budget line from zero rather than last year plus a percentage — understand when ZBB adds value and the process for justifying every cost.

steps.d: Create a spreadsheet that asks each cost center to justify every line item from zero — headcount, contractor spend, software licenses — rather than starting from last year.
For a given cost (office space, an engineering hire), require the owner to explain why this dollar is necessary and what it delivers.
Build the same budget two ways — ZBB (from zero) and incremental (last year + 3%) — and note where the two differ most.
Classify costs as fixed (lease, salary), variable (commissions, COGS), or discretionary (marketing, conferences) to spot opportunities to flex spending.
Choose whether ZBB, incremental, or hybrid makes sense for your function or company given the pace of change and how much reforecasting happens mid-year.

topics.title: Rolling Forecasts
topics.description: Replace the static annual budget with a 12-month rolling forecast that updates every period — design the cadence, ownership, and model structure.

steps.d: Define the schedule — reforecast monthly, quarterly, or twice a year — and determine who owns each forecast update and by when.
Create a spreadsheet where month 1 is always the current month; when a new month closes, delete month 13 and add a new month 12.
Document the key drivers (headcount growth, revenue per customer, COGS %) and define how quickly they change or stay constant in your forecast.
Each month, show the variance between last forecast and actual; identify which assumptions were wrong and adjust next forecast.
Track the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) for revenue, EBITDA, and headcount across months to see whether your forecasts are improving.

topics.title: Driver-Based Modelling
topics.description: Identify the two or three operational drivers that explain most of the revenue and cost movement, then build forecast models that update when those drivers change.

steps.t: Identify the top two or three business drivers
steps.d: For a SaaS company, pick ARR and churn; for a marketplace, pick take rate and GMV; for retail, pick same-store sales and headcount.
Create a forecast where revenue = units sold * price, and gross margin = revenue * contribution margin %, linking changes in drivers to P&L line items.
Project each driver independently using historical trends, management guidance, or macro assumptions (GDP growth, competitive intensity).
Show how a 5% rise in ARR and a 0.5pp increase in churn combine to drive a specific dollar change in net revenue retention.
Run scenarios: what if churn increases 1%, or price drops 10%, or headcount grows 20%? Show the P&L impact of each driver movement.

topics.title: Actual vs Budget Variance Analysis
topics.description: Compute price, volume, and mix variances, present them in a structured table, and write the narrative that explains the most material items.

steps.d: Calculate Actual - Budget for revenue, COGS, and OpEx, and rank them by dollar impact to find the biggest misses.

steps.t: Separate volume, price, and mix variance
steps.d: For a revenue miss, isolate how much came from lower volume (units), lower price, and unfavorable product mix.
For a cost overrun, calculate whether it was spending variance (paid more than expected) or volume variance (used more units than expected).
Focus your analysis on variances over a threshold (e.g., > $100k or > 10% of budget) and skip the noise of small items.
Create a one-page summary explaining the top three variances — what happened, why, and what changed in assumptions for next forecast.

topics.title: Waterfall Charts and Bridge Analysis
topics.description: Visualise how profit moved from budget to actual using a waterfall chart — build a bridge that shows the contribution of each variance driver.

steps.d: Create a chart showing Budget, then boxes for each variance driver, then Actual; each box shows the dollar contribution of that variance to closing the gap.

steps.t: Visualize the bridge from budget to actual
steps.d: Build a waterfall for revenue, a separate one for EBITDA, showing how volume, price, and cost variances combine to explain the total miss.
Choose colors so positive variances are green and negative are red, label each driver, and ensure the chart tells the story without spoken explanation.

steps.t: Add variance drivers to the waterfall
steps.d: For each bridge, show at least three drivers of variance (volume, price, cost, headcount) so the audience understands where the gap came from.
Confirm that Budget + all variance boxes = Actual, and that the sum of each variance column equals the total variance.

topics.title: Root Cause Analysis in Finance
topics.description: Go beyond reporting the number to explaining why — use structured root cause techniques to separate one-off items from systemic issues.

steps.d: Draw a fishbone for a negative variance (revenue miss) and fill in potential causes across categories: pricing, sales execution, market, product.
Document which variances were temporary (customer default, one-time expense) and which reflect an ongoing problem (rising churn, lower close rates).

steps.t: Trace a cost overrun to its source
steps.d: For a headcount or software spend overage, trace back through approval processes to find where the forecast assumption was wrong or a change was approved but not reflected in the budget.

steps.t: Quantify the impact of each root cause
steps.d: Assign a dollar impact to each identified root cause ('lost contract: -$500k', 'scope creep in engineering: +$150k') so the causes sum to the variance.
For each root cause, propose a specific change (weekly forecast update, approval gate, metric tracking) and explain how it fixes the problem.

topics.title: P&L Structure and Contribution Margin
topics.description: Build a management P&L from revenue through gross profit to contribution margin — understand what each line measures and how it drives decisions.

steps.d: Create a P&L that shows Revenue, less COGS, equals Gross Profit, then less variable OpEx (commissions, delivery), equals Contribution Margin.
Classify costs as fixed (salaries, rent) or variable (COGS, shipping) so you know which costs scale with revenue and which do not.
For each product line, compute contribution margin in dollars and as a % of revenue to see which products are actually profitable.
Show leadership that contribution margin funds fixed costs (overhead) and profit; higher contribution margin means more cash for growth and more resilience to downturns.
Track contribution margin % month-over-month to catch when unit economics deteriorate (COGS rising, mix getting worse) before profits collapse.

topics.title: EBITDA Walk
topics.description: Produce an EBITDA bridge that starts with revenue and adds back D&A, interest, and tax adjustments — the standard format for management and investor reporting.

steps.d: Start with net revenue at the top, add back depreciation and amortization, interest, and taxes to show what the business generates before financing and tax effects.
Show Revenue → Gross Profit → EBITDA → EBIT (after D&A) → EBT (after interest) → Net Income (after tax) in a single waterfall.
Show a rolling 12-month EBITDA bridge for each quarter so investors and leadership can see how recent trends compare to prior year.
Verify that your bridge from revenue to EBITDA matches the audited P&L, and document any adjustments (one-time items, stock-based comp) clearly.
Present an EBITDA bridge in a board meeting or investor update and explain how improvements in gross margin or OpEx leverage flow to EBITDA.

topics.title: KPI Dashboards
topics.description: Select the five to eight KPIs that matter most, design a one-page dashboard, and build the data flows that keep it updated each period without manual effort.

steps.t: Select 5 to 8 KPIs that drive decisions
steps.d: For your company, choose metrics that matter to leadership (ARR, churn, payback period, NRR) and exclude vanity metrics no one acts on.
Arrange headline metrics at the top (revenue, growth rate), add trend charts for each, and include red/yellow/green status indicators for quick scanning.
Set targets for each KPI based on historical performance, peer benchmarks, and strategic plans so the dashboard tracks progress toward goals.
Build a feed from source systems (accounting, CRM, operations) to a single model that updates nightly, so the dashboard refreshes without manual copy-paste.
Share the dashboard with leadership, gather feedback on what's missing or unclear, and adjust KPIs or visualizations based on how often each metric is actually used in decisions.

topics.title: Presenting to Leadership
topics.description: Structure a CFO or board-ready financial update — lead with the headline, quantify the impact, and anticipate the questions executives will ask.

steps.d: Lead with the headline metric and its status vs. target (ARR $5M, up 20% YoY, tracking to $6M forecast), then explain the key drivers below.
Instead of 'churn improved' say 'churn dropped from 3.5% to 3.2% this month, -0.3pp MoM', so listeners can judge materiality.
Before presenting to the CFO or board, list five questions they will ask (is this a one-off?, what changed?, will this persist?) and prepare data to answer each.
Design a standard format for financial presentations — headline, one chart, two supporting metrics, one data note — so the board knows what to expect.
Give your presentation to someone outside finance and time how long it takes; if you're over 5 minutes, cut or move lower-priority information to appendix.

topics.title: Narrative Frameworks for Finance
topics.description: Use frameworks like Situation-Complication-Resolution and the Pyramid Principle to turn a page of numbers into a coherent story that drives action.

steps.d: Start by stating the situation (YoY ARR grew 25%), then the complication (but churn rose 0.5pp), then your resolution (we are investing in retention because LTV payback improved).
Lead with your main conclusion ('we are ahead of plan'), then support it with 2-3 sub-conclusions (revenue is 5% above forecast, costs are flat), then details underneath.
Structure your update as: where we planned to be, where we actually are, why the gap exists, and what we'll do about it.

steps.t: Connect financial results to business decisions
steps.d: For each metric variance, explain what decision leadership should make based on it (increase marketing spend, pause hiring, renegotiate vendor contract).

steps.t: Test your narrative with a peer
steps.d: Tell your story to someone who hasn't seen the data and ask what action they would take based on what you said; refine until the implication is clear.

topics.title: Chart Selection for Financial Reporting
topics.description: Match the right chart type to each financial message — use bar charts for comparison, line charts for trends, and waterfall charts for bridges — and avoid the common mistakes that mislead audiences.

steps.d: Use grouped or stacked bars to compare revenue across regions, products, or time periods so viewers can visually rank them.
Plot monthly revenue, churn, or ARR as a line so the audience sees direction, acceleration, or volatility at a glance.
Show how budget variance breaks into volume, price, and cost components with a waterfall so each driver's magnitude is visible.
Don't truncate the y-axis to exaggerate changes, don't use 3D effects that distort perception, and don't mix conflicting metrics on one chart.
For a board presentation, choose one chart per slide, make it large, add a title that states the insight (not just 'Revenue Trend'), and remove clutter.

topics.title: Excel and Google Sheets Best Practices for FP&A
topics.description: Apply naming conventions, structured tables, and formula audit trails so your models are easy to hand over, review, and maintain under deadline pressure.

steps.d: Name ranges like assumptions, headcount, and cogs_rate so formulas read =assumptions.cogs_rate * revenue instead of =B$2*A5.
Create separate sheets for assumptions, data, calculations, and output so each tab has a single job and is easy to hand to someone else.
Add a column next to each formula showing the input references, the calculation, and the output so a reviewer can trace how a number was computed.
Verify each formula against a manual calculation on a simple example, then check edge cases (zero values, negative values) before deploying.
Create an assumptions tab that lists every key input (revenue growth rate, churn, tax rate) with the source, date, and owner so someone can update it later.

topics.title: Power Query for Finance Data
topics.description: Use Power Query to automate the monthly data pull — connect to source files, clean and reshape the data, and refresh the model with one click instead of hours of manual work.

steps.d: Use Power Query to link to an accounting export (CSV or Excel) and set a refresh schedule so the model pulls fresh data without manual import.
Apply transformations in Power Query (split columns, remove duplicates, pivot data) rather than in formulas so the source data stays clean.

steps.t: Map GL codes to reporting categories
steps.d: Load the chart of accounts and GL detail, then map each GL code to your reporting categories (headcount, rent, COGS) in Power Query.
Set up Power Query feeds for revenue, expenses, and headcount so clicking 'Refresh All' pulls the latest data and recalculates the P&L.
Write down which source files and GL accounts feed your model, the refresh frequency, and who to notify if a source breaks.

topics.title: Anaplan and Enterprise FP&A Platforms
topics.description: Understand the landscape of FP&A software — what Anaplan, Workday Adaptive, and Planful do that Excel cannot, and how to evaluate a tool for your organisation.

steps.t: Evaluate Anaplan, Workday Adaptive, and Planful
steps.d: Research each platform's strengths — Anaplan for complex modeling, Workday for integrated accounting, Planful for mid-market ease — and compare to Excel's flexibility.

steps.t: Assess when to move from Excel
steps.d: Build a decision matrix that weighs: number of users, collaboration needs, model complexity, and audit requirements to decide if a platform pays for itself.
Build your current budget or forecast model in a tool's free trial and time how long it takes versus your Excel process.
Factor in software license cost, implementation and training time, and ongoing support when comparing an FP&A platform to staying in Excel.
Document whether to stay in Excel, adopt a cloud planning tool, or move to an enterprise platform, and present a 12-month roadmap for the change.

topics.description: The ribbon, cells, sheets, and the keyboard habits that make everything else faster.

steps.d: Open each ribbon tab (Home, Insert, Data, Formulas) once and note the three or four commands you'll use most.
Use Ctrl+Arrow keys to jump to the edge of a data range, and Ctrl+Home to return to A1.
Select a whole column with Ctrl+Space and a whole row with Shift+Space instead of dragging.
Add a new sheet, rename its tab, and move between sheets with Ctrl+PageUp/PageDown.

steps.t: Freeze panes on a long sheet
steps.d: Freeze the header row on a large dataset so it stays visible while you scroll.

topics.title: The Excel Interface & Navigation

topics.description: Relative vs. absolute references, and why a dragged formula breaks without them.

steps.d: Enter =A2*B2 and drag it down a column, watching the row numbers update automatically.
Rewrite a formula with $B$1 so dragging it keeps pointing at one fixed tax-rate or fee cell.
Build a formula that locks the column but not the row (or vice versa) and drag it both across and down.
Write a formula that pulls a value from a different sheet, e.g. =Summary!B2.
Take a formula that returns the wrong value after being copied, and find which reference should have been absolute.

topics.title: Formulas & Cell References

topics.description: The handful of functions that cover most day-to-day spreadsheet work.

steps.d: Use =SUM(range) instead of adding cells one by one, and confirm it updates when a value changes.
Use =AVERAGE(range) on the same data and compare it to the total.
Write =IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) to label rows as "Over budget" or "On budget".
Use =COUNTIF(range, criteria) to count how many rows meet one condition.
Nest one function inside another, e.g. =IF(SUM(range)>1000, "High", "Low").

topics.title: Core Functions: SUM, AVERAGE, IF, COUNT

topics.description: Pull a value from another table by matching an id or name — the move behind every reconciliation, mapping table and report you will build.

steps.d: Put a small price list on one sheet and an order list on another; pull each price across with VLOOKUP and an exact match.
Rewrite the same lookup with XLOOKUP and note what got simpler: no column number, no exact-match flag, a built-in "not found" value.
Insert a column inside the lookup range and watch the VLOOKUP return the wrong field — then confirm XLOOKUP keeps working.

topics.title: Lookups: VLOOKUP & XLOOKUP

topics.description: Turn a range into a proper Excel table, then sort, filter and tidy it — the habits that keep a growing data set and every formula pointing at it from breaking.

steps.t: Convert a range to a table
steps.d: Select a small data set and press Ctrl+T; note the automatic banding, filters and a total row.
Sort by two columns at once, then filter to one category and read the totals.
Split a "First Last" name column into two columns with Flash Fill instead of a formula.

topics.title: Tables, Sorting & Filtering
